items.title: 21.7 Cosmic Redshift: Evidence for an Expanding Universe

source_refs.note: Topic 21.7 (PDF 175-176). Equation 21.4 printed with '>>' is corrected in a warning. The redshift example and check question are added; answers need review.

blocks.text: Cosmic redshift is the effect in which light from distant galaxies is stretched towards the red end of the spectrum. It happens because the universe is expanding, so galaxies are moving away from us and the wavelength of the light they emit increases. The greater the distance of a galaxy, the larger its redshift, that is, the faster it is moving away. By studying cosmic redshift, scientists can measure how fast the universe is expanding.

The observed change in wavelength is related to the relative velocity v between the source and the observer: z = dlambda/lambda = df/f = v/c (21.4). A positive dlambda indicates a redshift, showing that the object is moving away from Earth; a negative dlambda is a blueshift, showing that it is approaching. The light from faraway galaxies appears redder than expected because space itself is stretching as the universe expands, which also stretches the light waves. The redshift pattern is observed in all directions, which shows that the universe is expanding: it is not just that galaxies are moving apart through space, but that the space between them is increasing. These findings strongly support the Big Bang theory, which says the universe began in an extremely hot and dense state and has been growing ever since.
